title: California braces for its most widespread storm of fall | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

California is facing its most widespread threat of flooding rain, heavy mountain snow and gusty winds of fall from an incoming atmospheric river-fueled storm.

🌧️Track the storm in the CNN Weather app

Anatmospheric riveris pretty much what it sounds like: a long, narrow plume of moisture that can flow thousands of miles high up in the atmosphere, like a fire hose in the sky. Storms tap into that moisture and wring it out in the form of heavy rain and mountain snow.

California is likely to see plenty more atmospheric river-fueled storms in the weeks and months to come as a potentially historic superEl Niño boosts the state’s odds of a wet winter.

The storm will spread across California by Wednesday and linger through Thursday, with the threat of flooding rainfall stretching from the Bay Area down to Los Angeles and San Diego.

Northern California and the Pacific Northwest have already been battered by a series of storms over the weekend into Monday.

Massive wavespounded much of the Pacific Coast, damaging Monterey Bay’s historic Capitola Wharf, while floodwater as deep as 2 feet inundated Bay Area highways, and wind gusts up to 64 mph buffeted Sonoma County.

Parts of the state’s coastline are still dealing with lingering high surf, and the incoming storm could bring another surge of large waves Wednesday night into Thursday.

Here’s what else to expect this week.

Heavy downpours will arrive across the Bay Area and Central Coast beginning early Wednesday morning.

These areas are under a Level 2 of 4 risk for flooding rain Wednesday, according to the Weather Prediction Center. Rainfall totals of 1 to 2 inches are forecast across much of the region, with 3 to 5 inches possible in spots, especially in the coastal mountain ranges.

Much of the heaviest rain, including some thunderstorms, could fall in just three to six hours as the storm’s front moves through, including through the Bay Area’s morning commute.

The combination of intense downpours on top of saturated ground from recent storms could flood roads. Off and on showers, and possibly a few thunderstorms, will stick around through Thursday in the wake of Wednesday morning’s initial, heavier burst.

Farther inland, at least 1 inch of rain is likely across the Sacramento Valley and nearby Sierra Nevada foothills, with 2 inches or more possible in some areas Wednesday and Thursday.

The flooding rain threat will spread to Los Angeles, San Diego and surrounding mountain areas by late Wednesday night into Thursday morning. Parts of Southern California, including those metros, are under a Level 2 of 4 risk of flooding rain Thursday, according to the Weather Prediction Center.

Rainfall totals of 1 to 3 inches are possible across portions of Southern California with locally higher amounts of 3 to 5 inches possible on some mountain slopes.

The most impactful punch of heavy rain will only last a few hours from late Wednesday night through Thursday morning as it advances southward through Los Angeles.

Flooding is possible in urban areas and rockslides could tumble down on canyon roads. Recently burned areas could also be prone to flooding and debris flows, especially if thunderstorms bring short bursts of heavier rain. Burned ground can’t absorb as much water and intense rainfall rates can also loosen up soil, making it easier for rain to carry it downhill.

Cold air is also accompanying this storm, and winter storm warnings are posted for heavy snow in the Sierra Nevada, which, while beneficial for ski resorts, will cause major travel disruptions.

Mountain passes like Interstate 80 through Donner Pass will experience dangerous travel conditions beginning Wednesday with snow falling at rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour alongside gusty winds.

Up to a foot of snow could accumulate at elevations as low as 4,000 feet, with up to 3 feet likely in some mountain locations above 5,000 feet through Thursday night. A few high peaks could receive up to 4 feet.

Strong winds will also accompany the storm, with gusts of 30 to 50 mph possible in parts of the Bay Area and elsewhere in interior Northern California on Tuesday night and Wednesday. That could be strong enough to down a few trees and cause scattered power outages.
